l: those who compel circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 6
s: Those who compel circumcision are said to desire a good impression in the flesh and to do this so they will not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. They are said not to keep the law themselves, and they want the recipients circumcised so they may boast in their flesh.

l: circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 6
s: Circumcision is presented as something being pressed on the recipients by others for self-serving reasons. The text declares that in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything, and that even those who receive it do not keep the law.

l: cross of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 6
s: The cross of Christ is the one thing in which the author is willing to boast, and through it the world has been crucified to him and he to the world. Those who compel circumcision act in order to avoid being persecuted for it.

l: new creation, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 6
s: The new creation is named as what counts in Christ Jesus, in contrast to circumcision or uncircumcision, which are nothing. Those who walk by this rule are blessed with peace and mercy.

l: sowing and reaping, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 6
s: Sowing and reaping is used as a principle that whatever a man sows he will also reap, so God is not mocked. Sowing to the flesh reaps corruption, while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life, and the brothers are told they will reap in due season if they do not give up doing good.

l: 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greet the assembly of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, wishing them grace and peace. They give thanks to God for the Thessalonians, remembering their work of faith, labor of love, and perseverance of hope. The writers know the Thessalonians are chosen because the Good News came to them in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with much assurance. The Thessalonians imitated the writers and the Lord, received the word amid affliction with joy, and became an example to believers in Macedonia and Achaia. Their faith has become known everywhere, and others report how they turned from idols to serve a living and true God and wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, who delivers from the wrath to come.

l: Paul, 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, writes to the assembly of the Thessalonians and greets them with grace and peace. He says they always thank God for the Thessalonians, pray for them, and know they are chosen. He recalls how the group showed themselves among the Thessalonians for their sake, and notes that others report on the reception they received.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: The assembly is addressed as being in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and is remembered for its work of faith, labor of love, and perseverance of hope. It became imitators of the writers and of the Lord, receiving the word in much affliction with joy of the Holy Spirit, and became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. Its faith toward God has spread everywhere, and it turned from idols to serve a living and true God and to wait for his Son from heaven.

l: God, 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: God the Father is named, with the Lord Jesus Christ, as the one in whom the assembly exists and as the source of grace and peace. He is thanked always in the writers' prayers, and is called "our God and Father." He raised his Son from the dead, and is described as a living and true God whom the Thessalonians turned to serve.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: The Lord Jesus Christ is named with God the Father as the one in whom the assembly exists and as a source of grace and peace. The Thessalonians' hope is in him, and they imitated him. He is God's Son, whom God raised from the dead, whom the Thessalonians await from heaven, and who delivers us from the wrath to come.

l: Good News of God, 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: The Good News came to the Thessalonians not in word only but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with much assurance. They received it in much affliction with joy of the Holy Spirit, and from them the word of the Lord has been declared in Macedonia, Achaia, and every place.

l: 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: In this chapter the speaker, writing as "we" and naming Paul once, reminds the Thessalonian believers that their visit was not in vain. Despite earlier suffering and shameful treatment at Philippi, the group boldly told them the Good News of God, without flattery, greed, or seeking glory, and behaved gently like a nursing mother and exhorting like a father. They worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. The writer thanks God that the believers accepted the message as God's word, and notes they suffered from their own countrymen just as the assemblies in Judea suffered from the Jews, who are described as having killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets and driven the group out. The group longed to see the believers again, Paul tried more than once but Satan hindered them, and the believers are called their hope, joy, crown of rejoicing, and glory.

l: God, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: God approved the speakers and entrusted them with the Good News, and he tests their hearts and is witness to their motives. He calls the believers into his own Kingdom and glory, and his word works in those who believe.

l: Paul, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: Paul is named as one of the speakers who wanted to come to the Thessalonians, and says he tried once and again but Satan hindered them. The group with him suffered at Philippi, worked night and day, and behaved gently and blamelessly toward the believers.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: The believers received the message as God's word rather than men's, and it works in them. They became imitators of the assemblies in Judea by suffering the same things from their own countrymen. The speakers call them their hope, joy, crown of rejoicing, and glory before the Lord Jesus at his coming.

l: Good News of God, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: The Good News of God was told boldly amid much conflict by those entrusted with it, and was preached to the Thessalonians free of burden to them. The speakers were pleased to impart it along with their own souls, and they were forbidden by opponents to speak it to the Gentiles that they might be saved.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: He is called the Lord Jesus, whom certain Jews killed. The speakers are described as apostles of Christ, and the believers will be before him at his coming.

l: Jews, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: The Jews are described as having killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, driven the speakers out, and displeased God. They are said to be contrary to all men and to forbid speaking to the Gentiles so they may be saved, filling up their sins, and wrath has come on them to the uttermost.

l: 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: The authors explain that, unable to bear their separation any longer, they stayed behind at Athens alone and sent Timothy, their brother and God's servant in the Good News of Christ, to establish and comfort the Thessalonian believers in their faith. They recall having warned the believers beforehand that affliction was coming, and say they feared the tempter had tempted them and made their labor vain. Timothy has now returned with glad news of the believers' faith, love, and good memories of the authors, which comforts the authors in all their distress and affliction. The authors express thanksgiving and joy before God, pray night and day to see the believers and to perfect what is lacking in their faith, and ask God and the Lord Jesus to direct their way to them. They close by praying that the Lord will make the believers increase in love and establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of Jesus with all his saints.

l: Timothy, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: Timothy is described as the authors' brother and God's servant in the Good News of Christ, sent to establish and comfort the Thessalonians concerning their faith. He has just returned to the authors with glad news of the believers' faith and love, and of their good memories of the authors and longing to see them.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: Jesus is called Lord and is asked, together with God the Father, to direct the authors' way to the Thessalonians. His coming is anticipated, when he will come with all his saints and the believers' hearts are to be established blameless in holiness. The Good News is identified as the Good News of Christ.

l: God, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: God is called Father, and the authors give thanks to him for the joy they have over the Thessalonians. They ask him, with the Lord Jesus, to direct their way to the believers. The authors pray that the believers' hearts be established blameless in holiness before him, and Timothy is called his servant.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: The Thessalonians were sent Timothy to be established and comforted, and they were told beforehand that affliction would come. They have remained steadfast in faith and love, remember the authors well, and long to see them. The authors pray that they will increase and abound in love toward one another and all people.

l: Paul, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: The authors, unable to bear separation any longer, stayed alone at Athens and sent Timothy, and one author speaks in the first person of sending him to learn of the believers' faith for fear the tempter had tempted them. They were comforted by Timothy's report, rejoice and give thanks to God, and pray night and day to see the believers and perfect what is lacking in their faith.

l: afflictions (suffering of the believers and authors), 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: The authors say they were appointed to affliction and told the Thessalonians beforehand that they would suffer it, as indeed happened. Timothy was sent so that no one would be moved by these afflictions. The authors were comforted in their own distress and affliction through the believers' faith.

l: faith (of the Thessalonians), 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: Timothy was sent to establish and comfort the Thessalonians concerning their faith, and the authors feared the tempter might have undone it. Timothy's report of their faith brought the authors comfort in their affliction, and they say they live if the believers stand fast in the Lord. The authors pray night and day to perfect what is lacking in it.

l: 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: In Chapter 4, the writers exhort the Thessalonian brothers to keep walking in the way they were taught so as to please God, and to abound more and more. They state that God's will is their sanctification, including abstaining from sexual immorality, controlling their own bodies in honor, and not wronging a brother or sister, since the Lord is an avenger in these matters. They commend the believers' brotherly love toward all the brothers in Macedonia while urging them to abound further, lead a quiet life, mind their own business, and work with their own hands so they walk properly before outsiders and need nothing. The writers then address those who have fallen asleep, telling the believers not to grieve like those without hope, because God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus. They describe the Lord descending with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ rising first, and the living being caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air, and they close by telling the believers to comfort one another with these words.

l: God, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: God's will is declared to be the believers' sanctification, and he called them not for uncleanness but in sanctification. He has given his Holy Spirit to them, has taught them to love one another, and will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: The Lord Jesus is the one through whom the writers gave instructions, and the one in whom they exhort the believers. He is described as an avenger in matters of sexual immorality and wronging others, and as one who died and rose again. He will himself descend from heaven with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, and believers will be with him forever.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: The brothers are exhorted to abound more and more in pleasing God, to live in sanctification, and to lead a quiet life, doing their own business and working with their own hands. They are praised for loving all the brothers in Macedonia, and are told not to be ignorant about those who have fallen asleep so they don't grieve like those without hope. They are told to comfort one another with the words about the Lord's coming.

l: those who have fallen asleep (the dead in Christ), 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: Those who have fallen asleep in Jesus will be brought by God with him. The living will in no way precede them, and the dead in Christ will rise first at the Lord's coming.

l: the living believers at the Lord's coming, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: The living who are left until the Lord's coming will in no way precede those who have fallen asleep. After the dead in Christ rise first, they will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so will be with the Lord forever.

l: sanctification and sexual purity, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: Sanctification is stated to be God's will, including abstaining from sexual immorality and each person controlling his own body in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who don't know God. No one should take advantage of or wrong a brother or sister in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger, and whoever rejects this rejects God, who gave his Holy Spirit.

l: brotherly love, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: The writers say the believers need no one to write to them about brotherly love, because they are taught by God to love one another. They already show it toward all the brothers in Macedonia, yet are exhorted to abound in it more and more.

l: the Lord's coming and the resurrection of the dead, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 4
s: The Lord will descend from heaven with a shout, the voice of the archangel and God's trumpet, and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then the living believers will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and this teaching is given so the believers will not grieve without hope and will comfort one another.

l: 1 Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 addresses the brothers about the times and seasons, reminding them that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night, bringing sudden destruction on those who say "Peace and safety." The writer contrasts the brothers, who are children of light and of the day, with those of the night, and urges them to stay awake and sober, wearing faith, love, and the hope of salvation as armor. God has appointed them to obtain salvation through the Lord Jesus Christ, who died for them so that they may live with him whether awake or asleep. The letter then gives a series of exhortations: respect those who labor among them, be at peace, admonish the disorderly, support the weak, do not return evil for evil, rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks, and test all things. It closes with a prayer that the God of peace sanctify them completely, a request for prayer, greetings, a command that the letter be read to all, and a blessing of grace.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 5
s: He is the one through whom God appointed believers to obtain salvation, and he died for them so that they might live together with him whether they wake or sleep. His coming is the point at which the recipients' whole spirit, soul, and body are to be preserved blameless, and the letter closes with a blessing of his grace.

l: God, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 5
s: God did not appoint the recipients to wrath but to obtaining salvation through the Lord Jesus Christ. Called the God of peace, he is asked to sanctify them completely, and he is described as faithful: the one who calls them will also do it. Giving thanks in everything is said to be his will in Christ Jesus.

l: day of the Lord, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 5
s: The day of the Lord is said to come like a thief in the night, something the recipients already know well. It brings sudden destruction, like birth pains on a pregnant woman, on those who say "Peace and safety," but it should not overtake the brothers, who are not in darkness.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 5
s: The brothers are called children of light and of the day, not of the night or darkness, and are urged to be watchful and sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of the hope of salvation. They are told to respect their leaders, live at peace, and follow a list of exhortations. The writer asks for their prayers, tells them to greet one another with a holy kiss, and commands that the letter be read to all the holy brothers.

l: those who say peace and safety, 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 5
s: These people are saying "Peace and safety" when sudden destruction comes on them like birth pains on a pregnant woman. The text says they will in no way escape. They are linked to the rest who sleep and are drunk in the night.

l: Christian exhortations (ethical instructions), 1 Thessalonians, Chapter 5
s: The chapter gives many instructions: encourage and build each other up, respect and honor those who labor among them, and be at peace. It also tells them to admonish the disorderly, encourage the faint-hearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all. Further commands include not returning evil for evil, always rejoicing, praying without ceasing, giving thanks in everything, not quenching the Spirit, not despising prophecies, testing all things, holding to the good, and abstaining from every form of evil.

l: Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, together with Silvanus and Timothy, greets the assembly of the Thessalonians and thanks God for their growing faith and abounding love. They boast about the Thessalonians' perseverance through persecutions and afflictions, which they present as a sign of God's righteous judgment and of being counted worthy of God's Kingdom. The letter says God will repay affliction to those who afflict them and give relief to the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his angels in flaming fire. Those who don't know God or obey the Good News will pay the penalty of eternal destruction, while Jesus will be glorified in his saints. Paul and his companions pray that God will count the Thessalonians worthy of their calling and that the Lord Jesus' name will be glorified in them.

l: Paul, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, writing with Silvanus and Timothy, greets the Thessalonian assembly and says they are bound to thank God for them. He boasts about their perseverance in the assemblies of God and says he and his companions always pray that God will count them worthy of their calling.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: The assembly is addressed as being in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and is praised for faith that grows exceedingly and for abounding love. It endures persecutions and afflictions, is promised relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed, and is prayed for so that it may be counted worthy of its calling and glorify the name of Jesus.

l: God, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: God is thanked for the Thessalonians and is the source of grace and peace together with the Lord Jesus Christ. His righteous judgment is said to be shown in their suffering, he will repay affliction to their afflicters and give relief to the afflicted, and he is asked to count them worthy of their calling and fulfill every desire of goodness and work of faith.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: The Lord Jesus Christ is named with God the Father as a source of grace and peace and as the one in whom the assembly exists. He will be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire, punish those who don't know God, and be glorified in his saints and admired among believers. His name is to be glorified in the Thessalonians, and they in him.

l: those who afflict the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: These people afflict the Thessalonian believers. It is called a righteous thing with God to repay affliction to them.

l: those who don't know God or obey the Good News, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: These people will be punished by the Lord Jesus when he is revealed from heaven. They will pay the penalty of eternal destruction from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might.

l: righteous judgment of God, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: The Thessalonians' perseverance in suffering is called an obvious sign of God's righteous judgment, pointing to their being counted worthy of God's Kingdom. This judgment includes repaying affliction to the afflicters and giving relief to the afflicted.

l: persecutions and afflictions, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: The Thessalonians endure persecutions and afflictions, and their perseverance and faith in them are a reason for boasting in the assemblies of God. These sufferings are said to be for God's Kingdom, and relief is promised when the Lord Jesus is revealed.

l: revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: The Lord Jesus is to be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire. It brings relief to the afflicted believers and punishment to those who don't know God or obey the Good News, and he comes in that day to be glorified in his saints.

l: eternal destruction, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: Eternal destruction is the penalty that those who don't know God and don't obey the Good News will pay. It is described as separation from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might.

l: faith and love of the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians / Chapter 1
s: Their faith is said to grow exceedingly, and the love of each and every one of them toward one another abounds. These are the reasons Paul and his companions give thanks to God and boast about them.

l: Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: The writer addresses the brothers about the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ and their gathering to him, urging them not to be shaken by claims that the day of Christ has already come. He says that day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of sin, the son of destruction, is revealed. This figure exalts himself as God in the temple of God, is restrained for now, and acts by the working of Satan with lying wonders, deceiving those who refused the truth. God sends those people a powerful delusion so they will be judged. The writer gives thanks that God chose the brothers for salvation, tells them to stand firm in the traditions they were taught, and asks the Lord Jesus Christ and God the Father to comfort and establish them.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: The Lord Jesus Christ's coming and the gathering of believers to him is the subject of the chapter. The Lord will kill the lawless one with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming, and believers are called to obtain his glory. Together with God the Father, he is asked to comfort the readers' hearts and establish them in every good work and word.

l: God, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: God sends a powerful delusion on those who did not receive the love of the truth, so that they believe a lie and are judged. He chose the brothers from the beginning for salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief in the truth, and called them through the Good News. Called God our Father, he loved believers and gave them eternal comfort and good hope through grace.

l: man of sin, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: The man of sin, the son of destruction, will be revealed after the rebellion comes, and he opposes and exalts himself against all that is called God, sitting in the temple of God and setting himself up as God. Something is restraining him until his own season, and the one who restrains is to be taken out of the way. His coming is by the working of Satan with all power, signs, lying wonders and deception, and the Lord will kill him with the breath of his mouth.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: The brothers are asked not to be quickly shaken or troubled by any spirit, word or letter claiming the day of Christ has come, and are told not to let anyone deceive them. They are described as loved by the Lord and chosen by God from the beginning for salvation. They are told to stand firm and hold the traditions taught by word or letter, and the writer prays that their hearts be comforted and established.

l: day of Christ, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 2
s: Some claim, as if from the writer, that the day of Christ has already come, and the readers are told not to be shaken by this. The writer says it will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of sin is revealed.

l: Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3, Paul asks the brothers to pray that the word of the Lord spreads and that he and his companions are delivered from unreasonable and evil men, while expressing confidence that the Lord is faithful and will guard them. He commands the brothers in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ to withdraw from any brother who walks in rebellion and not after the tradition received from Paul and his companions. Paul points to his own example of working night and day so as not to burden anyone, and recalls the rule that anyone unwilling to work should not eat. He reports hearing of some who do not work but are busybodies, and commands them to work quietly and eat their own bread. He instructs the brothers not to grow weary in doing right, to note and avoid anyone who disobeys the letter yet admonish him as a brother, and closes with a greeting in his own hand and a blessing of peace and grace.

l: Paul, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord spread and that he be delivered from evil men, and commands the brothers to withdraw from those who walk in rebellion. He cites his own labor night and day as an example to imitate, and authenticates the letter by writing the closing greeting with his own hand as the sign in every letter.

l: Lord Jesus Christ, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: The Lord is described as faithful, establishing the brothers and guarding them from the evil one, and is invoked as the Lord of peace who gives peace at all times. Commands and exhortations are given in his name, and the letter closes with a blessing of his grace on all.

l: assembly of the Thessalonians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: The brothers are asked to pray for Paul, are credited with doing and continuing to do what is commanded, and are told to withdraw from rebellious brothers and to imitate Paul's example of work. They are urged not to grow weary in doing right and to admonish a disobedient brother as a brother, not as an enemy.

l: disorderly brothers (those who walk in rebellion), Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: Some among the brothers are reported to walk in rebellion, not working at all but being busybodies, contrary to the tradition received from Paul. They are commanded and exhorted to work with quietness and eat their own bread, and anyone who disobeys the letter is to be noted and shunned so that he may be ashamed, while still being admonished as a brother.

l: commands and tradition (Paul's teaching), Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: Paul commands in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ that the brothers withdraw from anyone not walking after the tradition they received from him. This teaching includes the earlier rule that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and disobedience to the word in this letter is to be noted and met with withdrawal of company.

l: work and self-support, Paul’s Second Letter to the Thessalonians, Chapter 3
s: Paul says he and his companions did not eat anyone's bread without paying, but labored night and day so as not to burden anyone, though they had the right to support, in order to set an example. The chapter commands that those who do not work should not eat, and that the idle should work quietly and eat their own bread.

l: Paul’s Letter to Philemon, Paul’s Letter to Philemon, Letter to Philemon / Chapter 1
s: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, writes with Timothy to Philemon, to Apphia, to Archippus, and to the assembly in Philemon's house, greeting them and thanking God for Philemon's love and faith. Paul says he could command Philemon but instead appeals out of love on behalf of Onesimus, whom he became father to in his chains. He is sending Onesimus back, asking Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, and offers to repay anything Onesimus owes. Paul expresses confidence in Philemon's obedience, asks him to prepare a guest room in hope of being restored to him through prayer, and relays greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke before closing with a blessing.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to Philemon, Letter to Philemon / Chapter 1
s: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, writes with Timothy to Philemon and the assembly in his house. He appeals rather than commands on behalf of Onesimus, sends him back, and promises in his own hand to repay anything Onesimus owes. He asks Philemon to prepare a guest room, hoping to be restored to him through prayer.

l: Philemon, Paul’s Letter to Philemon, Letter to Philemon / Chapter 1
s: Philemon is addressed as Paul's beloved fellow worker, praised for his love and faith toward the Lord Jesus and all the saints, and for refreshing the hearts of the saints. Paul appeals to him to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother rather than a slave, and to put any wrong or debt to Paul's account. Paul says Philemon owes him even his own self and expresses confidence that he will do even more than asked.

l: Onesimus, Paul’s Letter to Philemon, Letter to Philemon / Chapter 1
s: Onesimus is called Paul's child, whom Paul became father to in his chains. He was once useless to Philemon but is now useful to both Paul and Philemon, and Paul sends him back, describing him as his own heart. Paul asks that Philemon receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, in the flesh and in the Lord.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to Philemon, Letter to Philemon / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is named as the Lord, in whom Paul is a prisoner and from whom, with God the Father, grace and peace come. Philemon's faith is directed toward him, and the knowledge of every good thing is said to be in Christ Jesus. Paul grounds his boldness and his hope for refreshment in him, and closes by wishing his grace be with Philemon's spirit.

l: The Letter from James, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, writes to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion. He urges them to count trials as joy because the testing of their faith produces endurance, and to ask God for wisdom in faith without doubting. He contrasts the humble and the rich, warns that temptation comes from a person's own lust and not from God, and says lust conceives sin, which produces death. He reminds them that every good gift comes from the Father of lights, who gave birth to them by the word of truth. He closes by telling them to be swift to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger, to be doers of the word and not only hearers, and to practice pure religion by visiting the fatherless and widows and keeping unstained by the world.

l: James, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: James identifies himself as a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ and writes a letter of greeting to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion. He exhorts them about trials, wisdom, temptation, listening, and doing the word, and defines pure religion.

l: God, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: God gives wisdom liberally and without reproach to anyone who asks in faith. He cannot be tempted by evil and tempts no one, is the Father of lights from whom every good and perfect gift comes, and by his own will gave birth to believers by the word of truth. He promised the crown of life to those who love him.

l: twelve tribes in the Dispersion, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: The twelve tribes in the Dispersion are the addressees of the letter, greeted by James. They are called brothers and told to count trials as joy, ask God for wisdom, resist temptation, and be doers of the word.

l: testing of faith, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: The testing of faith is said to produce endurance, which is why James tells his readers to count various temptations as all joy. The person who endures temptation and is approved will receive the crown of life.

l: endurance, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: Endurance is produced by the testing of faith. James says it should have its perfect work so that believers may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

l: lust and sin, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: Temptation arises when a person is drawn away and enticed by his own lust, not by God. When lust has conceived it bears sin, and sin when full grown produces death.

l: word of truth, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: By the word of truth God gave birth to believers, making them a kind of first fruits of his creatures. The implanted word is to be received with humility and is able to save souls.

l: hearers and doers of the word, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: James tells his readers to be doers of the word and not only hearers who delude themselves. A mere hearer is like a man who looks at his natural face in a mirror and immediately forgets it, while the one who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues as a doer will be blessed in what he does.

l: religion, The Letter from James, The Letter from James / Chapter 1
s: James says that a person who thinks himself religious but does not bridle his tongue deceives his heart, and his religion is worthless. Pure and undefiled religion before God the Father is to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction and to keep oneself unstained by the world.

l: The Letter from James, The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 addresses the letter's readers, called brothers, and forbids them to hold the faith of the glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality. It illustrates this with a man in a gold ring and fine clothing who is given a good seat while a poor man in filthy clothing is told to stand or sit by a footstool, and it says God chose the poor to be rich in faith while the rich oppress and drag the readers into court. Partiality breaks the royal law, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' and whoever stumbles in one point of the law is guilty of all, so the readers must speak and act as people judged by the law of freedom, since judgment is without mercy to those who show none. The chapter then argues that faith without works is dead, using the example of a brother or sister left unfed with only kind words, the demons who believe and shudder, Abraham who offered Isaac, and Rahab the prostitute who received the messengers. It concludes that a man is justified by works and not only by faith, as the body without the spirit is dead.

l: God, The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: God is said to have chosen those who are poor in this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the Kingdom he promised to those who love him. He is the one whom the demons also believe to be one, and Abraham, who believed him, was called his friend.

l: Abraham, The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: Abraham is called 'our father' and is said to have been justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar. His faith worked with his works and was perfected by them, fulfilling the Scripture that he believed God and it was accounted to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.

l: Rahab, The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: Rahab the prostitute is given as a second example of someone justified by works. She received the messengers and sent them out another way.

l: twelve tribes in the Dispersion, The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: The brothers are told not to hold the faith with partiality, and are accused of dishonoring the poor man and of becoming judges with evil thoughts. They are reminded that the rich oppress them and drag them before the courts, and they are urged to fulfill the royal law, to speak and act as those judged by the law of freedom, and to show mercy and works along with their faith.

l: rich man (with gold ring), The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: The man with a gold ring and fine clothing is pictured coming into the synagogue and being given special attention and a good place to sit. The text also says that the rich oppress the readers, drag them before the courts, and blaspheme the honorable name by which they are called.

l: poor man (in filthy clothing), The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: The poor man in filthy clothing is pictured entering the synagogue and being told to stand there or sit by a footstool. The text says the readers have dishonored him, though God chose the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of the Kingdom.

l: partiality, The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: Partiality is forbidden in holding the faith of the Lord Jesus Christ and is shown in favoring the fine-clothed man over the poor man. It makes the readers judges with evil thoughts, is a sin, and convicts them by the law as transgressors.

l: royal law, The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: The royal law is identified with the Scripture 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' Fulfilling it is said to be doing well, while showing partiality breaks it and brings conviction as transgressors.

l: faith and works, The Letter from James, Chapter 2
s: Faith without works is called dead in itself, useless like kind words that give a hungry, poorly clothed brother or sister nothing, and no better than the belief of demons who shudder. The text says faith worked with Abraham's works and was perfected by them, that a man is justified by works and not only by faith, and that faith apart from works is dead like a body apart from the spirit.

l: The Letter from James, The Letter from James, Chapter 3
s: The author addresses his brothers, warning that not many should become teachers because teachers face heavier judgment and everyone stumbles in many ways. He argues that the tongue, though a small member like a horse's bit or a ship's rudder, boasts great things and can set a whole forest ablaze, defiling the whole body. Mankind has tamed every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature, but nobody can tame the tongue, a restless evil full of deadly poison that both blesses God and curses people made in God's image. Using the images of a spring, a fig tree, and a vine, the author says blessing and cursing should not come from the same mouth. He closes by contrasting earthly wisdom, marked by jealousy and selfish ambition, with wisdom from above, which is pure, peaceable, and full of mercy, and whose fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by peacemakers.

l: tongue, The Letter from James, Chapter 3
s: The tongue is described as a little member that boasts great things, likened to a horse's bit, a ship's rudder, and a small fire that spreads through a large forest. It is called a fire and a world of iniquity that defiles the whole body and is set on fire by Gehenna. Nobody can tame it, and it is a restless evil full of deadly poison, used both to bless God and to curse men.

l: twelve tribes in the Dispersion, The Letter from James, Chapter 3
s: The brothers are told that not many of them should be teachers, since teachers will receive heavier judgment, and that all stumble in many things. They are told that blessing and cursing from the same mouth ought not to be so, and are asked who among them is wise and understanding. They are urged to show good conduct in gentleness and not to boast or lie against the truth if they harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition.

l: God, The Letter from James, Chapter 3
s: God is called Father and is blessed with the tongue. The text notes that men, whom people curse with the same tongue, are made in the image of God.

l: blessing and cursing, The Letter from James, Chapter 3
s: Blessing and cursing are said to come out of the same mouth, with the tongue blessing God and Father and cursing men made in God's image. The author says these things ought not to be so, comparing it to a spring that cannot send out both fresh and bitter water, a fig tree that cannot yield olives, or a vine that cannot yield figs.

l: earthly wisdom, The Letter from James, Chapter 3
s: Earthly wisdom is identified with bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in the heart and is said not to come down from above. It is called earthly, sensual, and demonic, and where it is found there is confusion and every evil deed.

l: wisdom from above, The Letter from James, Chapter 3
s: Wisdom from above is described as first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality and without hypocrisy. Its fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

l: The Letter from James, The Letter from James, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 addresses readers whose quarrels and fights arise from their pleasures and lusts, and who fail to receive because they ask with wrong motives. It calls them adulterers and adulteresses, warning that friendship with the world is hostility toward God, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. It then commands the readers to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, mourn, and humble themselves so that the Lord will exalt them. It forbids speaking against and judging a brother, since only one lawgiver is able to save and destroy. Finally, it rebukes those who confidently plan to travel, trade, and profit for a year, reminding them that life is a vapor, that they should say 'If the Lord wills,' and that knowing the good and not doing it is sin.

l: God, The Letter from James, Chapter 4
s: God is described as the one whose enemy a friend of the world becomes, and the Spirit he caused to live in the readers is said to yearn jealously. He resists the proud, gives grace to the humble, draws near to those who draw near to him, and exalts the humble. He is the only lawgiver, able to save and to destroy, and his will governs whether people live and act.

l: twelve tribes in the Dispersion, The Letter from James, Chapter 4
s: The readers are accused of fighting, lusting, murdering, and coveting, and of asking with wrong motives so they do not receive. They are called adulterers and adulteresses, sinners, and double-minded, and are told to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse their hands, purify their hearts, mourn, and humble themselves. They are also warned against speaking against brothers, judging, and boasting about future plans.

l: world, The Letter from James, Chapter 4
s: Friendship with the world is declared hostility toward God. Whoever wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.

l: pleasures and wrong desires, The Letter from James, Chapter 4
s: Pleasures that war in the readers' members are named as the source of wars and fightings among them. Lust and coveting leave them without what they want, and asking with wrong motives to spend on their pleasures means they do not receive.

l: pride and humility, The Letter from James, Chapter 4
s: God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, according to the quoted Scripture. The readers are told to be subject to God and to humble themselves in the Lord's sight, and he will exalt them.

l: judging others, The Letter from James, Chapter 4
s: The readers are told not to speak against one another, because speaking against or judging a brother means speaking against and judging the law. Doing so makes one a judge rather than a doer of the law, and only the one lawgiver is able to save and destroy, so no one has standing to judge another.

l: boasting about future plans, The Letter from James, Chapter 4
s: Those who say they will go to a city, spend a year, trade, and make a profit are rebuked for not knowing what tomorrow holds, since life is a vapor that appears briefly and vanishes. They ought to say 'If the Lord wills,' and their boasting is called evil.

l: The Letter from James, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 opens by warning the rich to weep and howl over coming miseries: their riches are corrupted, their gold and silver corroded, and the wages they withheld by fraud from the laborers who mowed their fields cry out to the Lord of Armies. The rich are accused of living in luxury and of condemning and murdering the righteous one, who does not resist them. The text then turns to the brothers, urging patience until the coming of the Lord, as a farmer waits for the rains, and pointing to the prophets and Job as examples of endurance. It forbids swearing oaths, telling them to let their yes be yes and their no be no. It closes by directing the suffering to pray, the sick to call the elders to pray and anoint them with oil, and all to confess sins and pray for one another, citing Elijah's prayer about rain and the saving of a sinner who wanders from the truth.

l: the rich, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: The rich are told to weep and howl over miseries coming on them. They are accused of withholding wages by fraud, living in luxury and pleasure, and condemning and murdering the righteous one, who does not resist them.

l: laborers (who mowed the rich's fields), The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: The laborers who mowed the fields had their wages kept back by fraud. Their cries, along with those of the reapers, have entered the ears of the Lord of Armies.

l: God, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: The Lord is called the Lord of Armies and hears the cries of the defrauded reapers. His coming is at hand, the judge stands at the door, and he is shown as full of compassion and mercy in the outcome seen with Job.

l: twelve tribes in the Dispersion, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: The brothers are urged to be patient until the coming of the Lord, to establish their hearts, and not to grumble against one another. They are told to follow the prophets and Job as examples, to avoid oaths, to pray, sing, call the elders when sick, confess sins to one another, and turn back any who wander from the truth.

l: riches, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: The riches of the oppressors are described as corrupted, with garments moth-eaten and gold and silver corroded. The corrosion will testify against them and eat their flesh like fire, since they laid up treasure in the last days.

l: withheld wages, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: The wages of the laborers who mowed the fields were kept back by fraud. They cry out, and the cries have reached the Lord of Armies.

l: patience, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: Patience is commanded until the coming of the Lord, illustrated by the farmer waiting for the early and late rain. It is further exemplified by the prophets who suffered and by Job, whose perseverance is recalled, and those who endured are called blessed.

l: coming of the Lord, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: The coming of the Lord is said to be at hand, and the believers are to be patient until it. The judge stands at the door, which is the reason given for not grumbling against one another.

l: prayer, The Letter from James, Chapter 5
s: Prayer is prescribed for the suffering, and for the sick together with the elders' anointing with oil in the Lord's name. The prayer of faith will heal the sick and bring forgiveness, and the insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective, as shown by Elijah, who prayed that it would not rain, and then prayed again so that the sky gave rain.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: This document is a letter from Paul, an apostle and servant of Jesus Christ, to the believers in Rome, set out in sixteen chapters. It argues that salvation and righteousness come by faith in Jesus Christ, for Jew and Greek alike, and then draws out how believers should live. Paul opens by greeting the Romans, expressing longing to visit, and declaring he is not ashamed of the Good News, the power of God for salvation. He shows humanity under God's wrath for suppressing the truth (ch. 1), then argues that judging others is inexcusable and that Jews and Gentiles will be judged impartially, with a true Jew being one inwardly (ch. 2). Both are under sin, and all are justified freely by grace through redemption in Christ, not by works of the law (ch. 3). Abraham is the model, counted righteous by faith before circumcision (ch. 4). Justified believers have peace with God, and Adam's trespass is contrasted with Christ's act of righteousness, where grace abounds more (ch. 5). Paul rejects continuing in sin so grace may increase: believers, baptized into Christ's death, are dead to sin and alive to God, since sin's wages are death but God's gift is eternal life (ch. 6). Using a marriage analogy, he says believers have died to the law, which is holy yet exposes sin, and he describes an inner struggle and deliverance through Jesus Christ (ch. 7). Life in the Spirit brings no condemnation, sonship, hope amid suffering, and the assurance that nothing can separate believers from God's love in Christ (ch. 8). Paul then grieves for his kinsmen Israel, discussing God's election, mercy, and a saved remnant, while Gentiles attained righteousness by faith (ch. 9). He prays for Israel's salvation, saying Christ fulfills the law and that confessing Jesus as Lord and believing in the resurrection saves everyone who calls on him (ch. 10). God has not rejected Israel; using the olive tree image, he warns Gentiles against boasting and says all Israel will be saved, praising God's wisdom (ch. 11). The closing chapters turn practical: present bodies as a living sacrifice, use differing gifts in one body, love sincerely, and overcome evil with good (ch. 12). He instructs submission to authorities, paying what is owed, and love as fulfilling the law (ch. 13), and urges acceptance of the weak in faith over food and days without judging (ch. 14). Paul asks the strong to bear with the weak, describes his ministry to the Gentiles, and announces his trip to Jerusalem with a contribution and his plan to visit Rome on the way to Spain (ch. 15). The letter ends by commending Phoebe, greeting many named individuals including Prisca, Aquila, Andronicus, and Junia, warning against divisive people, and passing on greetings from Timothy, Tertius (who wrote the letter), and others, with a final blessing of grace (ch. 16).

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Paul is the writer of a letter to believers in Rome, presenting himself as a servant of Jesus Christ, a called apostle set apart for the Good News, and specifically an apostle to the Gentiles who serves as priest of that Good News. He is an Israelite, descended from Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin, and he feels great, unceasing sorrow for his Israelite relatives, hoping to provoke them to jealousy and save some. The records open with his self-introduction, his grace and commission from God, his debt to Greeks and foreigners, and his lack of shame about the Good News. He thanks God for the Romans, prays for them, and has long wanted to visit but was often hindered. He then reasons about Israel's stumbling, God's faithfulness, and the mystery of Israel's partial hardening, warning Gentile readers against conceit. Later he explains his aim to preach where Christ was not named, having preached from Jerusalem around to Illyricum without building on another's foundation. He plans to carry a contribution to Jerusalem, then go to Spain by way of Rome, and asks prayer for deliverance from the disobedient in Judea. The letter ends with commendation of Phoebe, many personal greetings, a warning against those causing divisions, relayed greetings, and a blessing of grace.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Jesus Christ, called 'our Lord', is presented in these records as the Son of God, descended from David and Israel according to the flesh, and declared Son of God with power by the resurrection. He is also described as over all, God, blessed forever. The records open with his identity and Paul's grace and apostleship received through him. They then turn to his saving work. God sent him as an atoning sacrifice, and righteousness comes by faith in him. He was delivered up for trespasses and raised for justification. He died for the ungodly, sinners and enemies, at the right time. Through him believers have peace with God, access into grace, and reconciliation. He is set against Adam as the one man whose obedience brings justification to life. Believers are baptized into his death. He was raised through the Father's glory, death no longer has dominion over him, and he lives to God. In him there is no condemnation. Believers die to the law through his body and are joined to the risen one. He sits at God's right hand interceding for believers, is firstborn among many brothers, and believers are joint heirs with him. He is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to all who believe, and confessing Jesus as Lord is part of being saved. He is the stumbling stone laid in Zion, yet those who believe in him will not be disappointed. In him the many are one body. He is Lord of both the dead and the living, all will stand before his judgment seat, and a fellow believer is one for whom he died. Readers are exhorted to put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Finally, he did not please himself, accepted believers to the glory of God, and became a servant of the circumcision to confirm the promises to the fathers so the Gentiles might glorify God. Paul boasts in his work through him for Gentile obedience. The records close with greetings from the assemblies of Christ and an invocation of his grace.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: God is presented in these records as the Creator, Father of believers, and the God of both Jews and Gentiles. He is eternal, the only wise God, true, impartial, just, patient, and the source of all things ('of him, through him, to him'). He is also called the God of perseverance and encouragement, of hope, and of peace. His power and divinity are seen in creation, and the Good News was promised beforehand through his prophets. The most important point is that he sent and raised his Son Jesus Christ as an atoning sacrifice, so that he is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith. He justifies the ungodly, counts righteousness apart from works, gives life to the dead, and pours his love into believers' hearts through the Holy Spirit. The account unfolds in stages. It begins with God revealing his righteousness in the Good News and his wrath against ungodliness, giving up those who rejected him. It then turns to his impartial judgment: he pays back each according to works, his goodness and patience lead to repentance, and he will judge secrets by Jesus Christ. Next come justification by faith, Abraham's promise, reconciliation through Christ's death, and the gift of eternal life. Sending his Son did what the law could not do. He foreknew, predestined, called, justified and glorified those he chose, and no one can stand against them. The records then address his sovereign right over creation like a potter over clay, his endurance of vessels of wrath, and his preparing of vessels of mercy. Israel is not rejected: a remnant is reserved, his gifts and calling are irrevocable, he is able to graft Israel in again, and he has bound all to disobedience to have mercy on all. The closing sections cover practical life under God: presenting oneself to him, proving his good and perfect will, the measure of faith he apportions, his vengeance belonging to him, and authorities ordained by him. He accepts both the one who eats and the one who doesn't, and every knee will bow to him. The records end by calling him the eternal, only wise God, the God of hope and peace, who will quickly crush Satan under believers' feet.

l: Rome, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: has_residents believers in Rome (the recipients of Paul's letter) Rome is the city where the letter's recipients live, who are beloved of God and called to be saints. Paul is eager to preach the Good News there and hopes to come to them, having been hindered so far.

l: believers in Rome (the recipients of Paul's letter), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Believers in Rome are beloved of God, called saints belonging to Jesus Christ, whose faith is proclaimed worldwide. Paul longs to impart a spiritual gift so they and he may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith.

l: the Good News, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The Good News is God's message about his Son, promised beforehand through the prophets in the Scriptures. It is God's power for salvation for everyone who believes, Jew first and Greek, and reveals God's righteousness from faith to faith. Paul, set apart for it, first longs to preach it in Rome; later he serves it as a priest, has preached it from Jerusalem to Illyricum, and aims to reach unevangelized places before coming to Rome.

l: Holy Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The Holy Spirit, called the Spirit of God, is given to believers and dwells in those in Christ Jesus. He gives the law of life freeing them from sin and death, and will give life to mortal bodies. He leads God's children, gives adoption, testifies with their spirits, and intercedes for their weakness. Believers hold Him as first fruits.

l: Jesus's resurrection and death, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father. Believers united with him in the likeness of his death will also be part of his resurrection, and they believe they will live with him.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The Gentiles are the non-Jewish peoples, set alongside Jews throughout the records. They lack the law yet act by nature as a law to themselves, with the work of the law written in their hearts and conscience accusing or excusing them. Called Greeks in places, they are, with Jews, all under sin, but God is their God too and justifies the uncircumcised through faith. Though they did not pursue righteousness, they attained the righteousness of faith, and some were called as God's people. Through Israel's fall they received salvation and mercy, pictured as a wild olive grafted contrary to nature into the olive tree, sharing its root. They are warned not to boast, since they stand by faith and could be cut off. Their fullness must come in before Israel's hardening ends. Finally, they are shown praising God, hoping in Jesse's root, and, having shared the Jerusalem saints' spiritual things, owing them material service, which Macedonia and Achaia have given.

l: Jews, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Jews are a group addressed as bearing the name, resting on the law, and glorying in God, yet charged with failing to practice what they teach, causing God's name to be blasphemed among Gentiles. A true Jew is redefined as one inwardly, circumcised in heart and praised by God. They hold priority in judgment, alongside Greeks, and a great advantage: entrustment with God's revelations. Still, Jews and Greeks alike are under sin, and God is not God of Jews only.

l: salvation, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Salvation is the speaker's prayer for Israel, coming to those who confess with the mouth that Jesus is Lord, believe God raised him from the dead, and call on the Lord's name; it is nearer now than at first belief.

l: righteousness of God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The righteousness of God is a righteousness revealed in the Good News and received through faith. Chapter 1 says it is revealed from faith to faith, citing that the righteous shall live by faith. Chapter 3 says it is revealed apart from the law, though the law and prophets testify to it, and comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe, showing God just and justifier. Chapter 10 contrasts it with Israel's own law-based righteousness, which they did not submit to, and ties it to heart belief.

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Faith is presented as the means by which God's righteousness reaches all who believe. In Chapter 1, the Romans' faith is proclaimed worldwide, and the Good News brings salvation through it, with Paul aiming at the obedience of faith among nations. Chapter 3 says faith justifies apart from works, excludes boasting, and covers circumcised and uncircumcised alike. Chapter 10 says it comes by hearing God's word, though not all listened. It establishes the law rather than nullifying it.

l: God's wrath, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: God's wrath is revealed from heaven against ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth; it unfolds as God giving them up to uncleanness, vile passions, and a reprobate mind, deeming such practices worthy of death.

l: ungodly people who suppress the truth, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: A group of people who knew God through creation and revelation yet refused to glorify or thank him. They grew vain and darkened in heart, claimed wisdom but became fools, and practiced idolatry. God gave them up to uncleanness, vile passions and a reprobate mind; they practice vices and approve others who do.

l: idolatry, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_a exchange of the truth of God for a lie Idolatry is described as trading the glory of the incorruptible God for images resembling corruptible man, birds, four-footed animals, and creeping things. It is also described as exchanging the truth of God for a lie and worshiping the creature rather than the Creator. God gave people up to uncleanness as a result.

l: same-sex relations, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Same-sex relations appear in Chapter 1 as part of God giving people up to vile passions: women exchange natural function for what is against nature, men burn in lust toward one another, and the men receive the due penalty of their error.

l: vices, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_deemed worthy of death [by God's ordinance] The text lists vices of those given up to a reprobate mind: unrighteousness, sexual immorality, wickedness, covetousness, malice, envy, murder, strife, deceit, evil habits, slander, backbiting, hatefulness to God, insolence, arrogance, boastfulness, inventing evil things, disobedience to parents, senselessness, covenant breaking, lack of natural affection, unforgiveness, and unmercifulness. It says those who practice such things are worthy of death, and that people both do them and approve of others who do.

l: law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The law is a standard addressed to Jews and those under it. Hearing it does not make anyone righteous; only doers are justified, while those who sin under it are judged by it. Its work is even written in Gentiles' hearts. It closes every mouth, brings the whole world under God's judgment, and gives knowledge of sin, so no flesh is justified by its works. Yet it testifies to God's righteousness, and faith establishes rather than nullifies it. It did not bring the promise to Abraham, since that would void faith. Instead it produces wrath, and believers are not under it.

l: judgment of God, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: God's judgment is truthful and righteous, falling on evildoers, Jew or Greek; hardened, unrepentant people store up wrath for the day of wrath, while well-doing earns eternal life, glory, honor, peace, and secrets are judged by Jesus Christ.

l: man (the one who judges), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: A man who judges others is declared without excuse, since he condemns himself by practicing the same things. Questioned about escaping God's judgment and despising His goodness, his hard, unrepentant heart is treasuring up wrath for himself.

l: circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Circumcision is a sign whose value depends on obeying the law: it profits doers but becomes uncircumcision for transgressors. The uncircumcised who keep ordinances are counted as circumcised, and true circumcision is of the heart, in spirit, not outward letter.

l: eternal life, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_a free gift of God [in Christ Jesus] Eternal life is the result of being freed from sin and becoming servants of God. It is described as the free gift of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, in contrast to the death that is the wages of sin.

l: justification, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Justification is presented as a status before God that cannot be obtained by works of the law; no flesh is justified that way. It is given freely by God's grace through redemption in Christ Jesus and received by faith apart from works. The account begins with this principle, then illustrates it with Abraham, whose belief was credited as righteousness while uncircumcised, with circumcision a seal. It extends to those who believe in him who raised Jesus. Believers are justified by faith and Christ's blood, gaining peace with God and assurance of salvation from wrath, as one act of righteousness brings life to all. Freed from sin, they become servants of righteousness, aiming at sanctification. Finally, Gentiles attained the righteousness of faith while Israel, pursuing it by works, stumbled.

l: sin, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Sin is presented as a universal power affecting the world: all, Jews and Greeks alike, have sinned and fall short of God's glory, and the law brings knowledge of it. It entered through one man, bringing death to all; it existed before the law but is not charged without law. It reigns in death and enslaves as a master, paying wages of death. Grace abounds more, so believers, who died to sin, are not under its dominion.

l: Abraham, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Abraham is presented as a forefather according to the flesh, counted righteous because he believed God rather than through works. He received circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith he held while uncircumcised. Thus he becomes father of many nations, of all who believe, and of the circumcised who walk in his faith. Though about a hundred years old, he did not waver, grew strong in faith, was fully assured of God's promise, and was promised to be heir of the world, with offspring through Isaac.

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Faith is the means by which righteousness is accounted to those who believe rather than work. In Chapter 4, Abraham's unweakened faith was counted as righteousness, and because the promise rests on faith, it accords with grace and is sure to all his offspring. In Chapter 5, faith justifies believers, gives access into grace, and brings peace with God through Jesus Christ.

l: works, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: produces reward as something owed [for him who works, not grace] Works are set against faith as a basis for justification. If Abraham were justified by works he would have something to boast about, though not toward God, and the reward for one who works is counted as something owed, not as grace. David pronounces blessing on the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works.

l: grace, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Grace is the standing and realm in which believers live, accessed by faith. In Chapter 5 it abounds through Jesus Christ far more than sin and trespass, reigning through righteousness to eternal life. Chapter 6 says believers live under grace, not law, rejecting sinning to magnify grace; sin will not dominate them.

l: circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_a sign [seal of the righteousness of faith] Circumcision was received by Abraham as a sign and a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised. Righteousness was not counted to him in circumcision. Abraham is father of the circumcised who also walk in the steps of his faith.

l: uncircumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_state_of Abraham [when faith was counted to him as righteousness] Abraham's faith was accounted to him for righteousness while he was in uncircumcision, not in circumcision. This makes him father of all who believe though uncircumcised, so that righteousness may be accounted to them also. The blessing is therefore not pronounced only on the circumcised.

l: promise, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_sure_to all the offspring [both of the law and of the faith of Abraham] The promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world came through the righteousness of faith, not the law. It is of faith so that it may be according to grace and sure to all the offspring, both those of the law and those of Abraham's faith. It includes the word "So will your offspring be," which Abraham believed against hope, and he was fully assured that God was able to perform it.

l: Adam, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Adam is the one man through whom sin entered the world, followed by death. Though a foreshadowing of Jesus Christ, his single trespass brought condemnation to all and made many sinners, with death reigning from him until Moses.

l: believers (those in Christ Jesus), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Believers, those in Christ Jesus, are a group defined by being justified by faith through Christ's blood. Once weak, ungodly sinners and enemies, they are reconciled to God through the death of his Son. They have peace with God, access into grace, and rejoice in hope of God's glory, even amid suffering. They are saved from wrath and face no condemnation. Led by the Spirit, they are children and heirs of God, joint heirs with Christ if they suffer with him. They hold the Spirit's first fruits and await adoption and bodily redemption. They are more than conquerors, and nothing can separate them from God's love.

l: death, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Death is a consequence of sin: it entered through sin, passed to all humanity because all sinned, and reigned from Adam until Moses. Believers who died with Christ are freed from sin; Christ died once and death no longer rules him, while grace brings life through him.

l: reconciliation, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Believers were reconciled to God while enemies, through the death of his Son. Being reconciled, they will be saved by his life, and they have now received the reconciliation through Jesus Christ, in whom they rejoice in God.

l: humanity (all men), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Humanity is described as condemned and subject to death through Adam's one trespass, yet justified to life through Jesus Christ's one act of righteousness; many become sinners, then many will be made righteous.

l: believers (the readers addressed), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The believers are the readers addressed in Chapter 6. They were once bondservants of sin but were baptized into Christ's death, united with him, and crucified their old man. Now dead to sin and alive to God, under grace rather than law, they obey the teaching from the heart. Freed from sin, they become servants of righteousness and of God, bearing sanctification's fruit, with eternal life as the result and a future share in resurrection.

l: baptism, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Baptism unites believers with Christ into his death, burying them with him, so that, as Christ was raised, they may walk in newness of life.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The law is holy, righteous, good, and spiritual, and is not itself sin. It holds dominion over a person only as long as he lives, and believers are discharged from it by dying to it. It reveals sin, including coveting, though sin used its commandment to produce death. The narrator delights in it inwardly. All its commandments are summed up in loving your neighbor as yourself, and love fulfills it.

l: sin, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Sin is a power dwelling in the narrator's flesh that, seizing occasion through the good commandment, produces coveting, deceives and kills him, and through a law in his members wars against his mind, holding him captive.

l: narrator (the speaker, "I"), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The narrator addresses the brothers, explains that he would not have known sin or coveting except through the law, and says he was once alive apart from the law but died when the commandment came. He describes doing what he hates and not doing what he desires, concluding that sin dwelling in his flesh is responsible. He cries out as a wretched man seeking deliverance, thanks God through Jesus Christ, and states that he serves God's law with his mind but sin's law with his flesh.

l: brothers (addressees), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The brothers are addressed as men who know the law. They are told that they were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, joined to him who was raised from the dead, and discharged from the law so that they serve in newness of the spirit rather than oldness of the letter.

l: flesh, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The flesh is portrayed as a realm whose mind is death, hostile to God, unsubmissive to His law, and unable to please Him; living after it leads to death, the law was weakened through it, yet God condemned sin in it.

l: law, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The law is weak through the flesh and could not do what God did through his Son. Its ordinance is nonetheless fulfilled in believers who walk according to the Spirit, while the flesh's mind is not subject to it; the Spirit's law contrasts with sin and death.

l: creation, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Creation was subjected to vanity, not by its own will, but in hope. It waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed, groaning together in pain until now, awaiting deliverance from the bondage of decay into glory.

l: love of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: cannot_be_separated_from believers (those in Christ Jesus) [nothing created can separate] The love of Christ is the thing from which the chapter asks who could separate believers, naming oppression, anguish, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril and sword. The text answers that believers are more than conquerors through him who loved them. Nothing, including death, life, angels, powers, height, depth or any created thing, can separate them from God's love in Christ Jesus.

l: Israel, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Israel is a people privileged with adoption, glory, covenants, the giving of the law, service, promises and the fathers, and the line from which Christ came according to the flesh. Yet not all of Israel are truly Israel; only a remnant is saved. Pursuing a law of righteousness by works rather than faith, Israel stumbled over the stumbling stone. It has zeal for God without knowledge, is ignorant of God's righteousness, and seeks to establish its own, remaining a disobedient and contrary people to whom God stretched out his hands. The speaker prays for its salvation. Its chosen obtained what it sought while the rest were hardened. Its fall brought salvation and riches to the Gentiles, and a partial hardening lasts until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in. Finally, all Israel will be saved: enemies for the Gentiles' sake regarding the Good News, but beloved for the fathers' sake regarding election.

l: children of the promise, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: are_counted_as heirs [as distinct from children of the flesh] The children of the promise, not the children of the flesh, are counted as heirs and as children of God. This is shown by Isaac, born by a word of promise to Sarah, and by Rebekah's son Jacob, since Abraham's offspring are not all children and the offspring is accounted through Isaac.

l: divine election, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: depends_on him who calls [not on works] God's purpose according to election stands not by works but by him who calls, as shown when Rebekah was told before her sons were born or had done good or bad that the elder would serve the younger. Paul cites 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated' and says vessels of mercy were prepared beforehand for glory and called from Jews and Gentiles.

l: God's mercy and hardening, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_exercised_according_to God's desire [he has mercy on whom he desires and hardens whom he desires] God declares to Moses that he will have mercy on whom he has mercy, so the outcome depends not on human will or running but on God. Pharaoh was raised up to display God's power and proclaim his name, and Paul concludes that God has mercy on whom he desires and hardens whom he desires, rejecting the objection that this makes God unrighteous.

l: believers (everyone who believes), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Believers are everyone who believes: they call on the Lord and receive salvation, gain righteousness through Christ, and are not disappointed. No Jew-Greek distinction exists; faith comes by hearing the preached word from those sent.

l: remnant, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: exists_according_to election of grace [at the present time] A remnant exists at the present time according to the election of grace, paralleling the seven thousand men God reserved in Elijah's day who had not bowed to Baal. The chosen ones within Israel obtained what Israel sought, while the rest were hardened.

l: olive tree, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: has_part natural branches [some broken off by unbelief] The olive tree is the image in which the root is holy and the branches are holy.
