Some natural branches were broken off by unbelief, and Gentiles, a wild olive, were grafted in to share the root and richness. The natural branches can be grafted back into their own tree if they do not continue in unbelief.

l: grace, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: excludes works The remnant exists according to the election of grace. The text states that if election is by grace it is no longer of works, otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

l: hardening of Israel, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: A partial hardening of Israel: those other than the chosen were given a spirit of stupor, unseeing eyes and unhearing ears per Scripture; it lasts until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, then all Israel will be saved.

l: salvation, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: has_come_to Gentiles [by Israel's fall, to provoke jealousy] Salvation has come to the Gentiles by Israel's fall, intended to provoke Israel to jealousy. The writer hopes to save some of his own people, and says all Israel will be saved when the Deliverer comes out of Zion and takes away their sins.

l: brothers (the addressees), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_part_of body of Christ (the church as one body) [individually members of one another] The brothers are urged to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, to be transformed by renewing their minds, and to think of themselves reasonably. They receive a series of commands on love, humility, hospitality, peace, blessing persecutors, and refusing revenge, ending with the charge to overcome evil with good.

l: this world, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: should_not_be_conformed_to_by brothers (the addressees) [instead transformed by renewed mind] This world is the pattern believers are told not to be conformed to. Transformation by the renewing of the mind is set against it.

l: body of Christ (the church as one body), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The church is one body in Christ, whose many members have differing functions yet belong to one another; unity and diversity are held together.

l: spiritual gifts, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: differ_according_to grace [given to us] Gifts differ according to the grace given to believers. The text names prophecy, service, teaching, exhorting, giving, ruling, and showing mercy. Each is to be used faithfully: prophecy in proportion to faith, giving with generosity, ruling with diligence, and mercy with cheerfulness.

l: living sacrifice (the believers' bodies), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Believers are urged to present their bodies as a living sacrifice that is holy and acceptable to God. The text calls this their spiritual service.

l: love, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: has_attribute without hypocrisy Love is to be without hypocrisy. It shows in tender affection among the brothers, preferring one another in honor, and blessing rather than cursing persecutors.

l: evil, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: should_be abhorred [believers' stance] Evil is something believers are told to abhor and never to repay with evil. They are not to be overcome by it but to overcome it with good.

l: the good (those who do good), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: should_be clung to [believers' stance] Good is what believers are told to cling to. It is the means by which evil is to be overcome, including feeding a hungry enemy and giving him a drink.

l: higher authorities, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Higher authorities are ordained by God, the source of all authority, and serve him for the reader's good. They are no terror to those who do good but bear the sword not in vain, avenging wrath on evildoers, and receive taxes as God's service.

l: Roman believers (the letter's recipients), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: The Roman believers are the recipients of Paul's letter, addressed across chapters 13, 15 and 16. They are instructed to submit to authorities, pay taxes, customs, respect and honor, and owe only love. They are urged to awaken, cast off darkness, and put on the armor of light and the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul urges them to bear with the weak, accept one another as Christ did, and be of one mind. He considers them full of goodness and knowledge, able to admonish others. He hopes to visit them on his way to Spain and asks for prayer. Finally they are asked to welcome Phoebe, avoid dividers, and be wise in good; their obedience is known to all, and God will crush Satan under their feet.

l: love, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Love is the one debt readers owe each other; it does no harm to a neighbor, sums up the commandments in loving one's neighbor as oneself, and thus fulfills the law.

l: subjection to authority, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Subjection is commanded of every soul, because resisting authority means withstanding God's ordinance and brings judgment. The readers are to submit not only because of wrath but also for conscience' sake, which includes paying taxes and giving respect and honor as owed.

l: one who is weak in faith, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: eats only vegetables [dietary habit] He is to be accepted, though not for disputes over opinions, and he eats only vegetables. He is told not to judge the one who eats, for God has accepted that person, and he is warned that if he eats while doubting, he is condemned because it is not of faith.

l: one who has faith to eat all things, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: eats all things [dietary habit based on faith] He has faith to eat all things and is told not to despise the one who abstains. He is urged not to destroy a brother with his food or cause a stumbling block, and to keep his own faith between himself and God. Though all things are clean, it is evil for him to cause stumbling by eating.

l: brother (the fellow believer), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: belongs_to Jesus Christ [whether living or dying] The brother is someone for whom Christ died, and no one should judge or despise him. He must not be grieved, made to stumble, offended, or weakened by another's food, and believers are to build one another up toward peace.

l: judging and despising others, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_answered_by judgment seat of Christ [all will stand before it] Judging and despising are forbidden: the one who eats must not despise the one who doesn't, and the one who doesn't must not judge the one who eats. The text asks why one would judge or despise a brother, since all will stand before Christ's judgment seat and each will give account to God. Believers are told instead to judge only that no one puts a stumbling block in a brother's way.

l: dietary practices (eating food, meat, wine), Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Dietary practices: some eat everything, others only vegetables, each honoring the Lord with thanks. Nothing is unclean in itself, only to one who deems it so. God's Kingdom is righteousness, peace, joy, not eating and drinking; abstaining is good if it prevents stumbling, and doubtful eating is sin.

l: saints at Jerusalem, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_a poor recipients of contribution [from Macedonia and Achaia] The saints at Jerusalem include the poor among them, for whom Macedonia and Achaia gladly made a contribution. The Gentiles are described as their debtors because they have shared in their spiritual things. Paul hopes his service will be acceptable to them.

l: Jerusalem, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_destination_of Paul's service to the saints [Paul going there now] Paul says he is going to Jerusalem to serve the saints, and it is the starting point of the region in which he has fully preached the Good News as far as Illyricum. He asks for prayer that his service for Jerusalem be acceptable.

l: Spain, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Spain is named as Paul's next destination, since he has no more place in the regions where he has worked. He hopes to see the Roman believers on his way there and be helped onward by them.

l: contribution for the poor saints, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: A gift gladly given by Macedonia and Achaia for the poor saints at Jerusalem; Paul frames it as a Gentile debt for spiritual blessings and plans to deliver it before traveling to Spain.

l: Paul's planned journey to Rome and Spain, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Paul's planned journey to Spain, passing through Rome. He must first go to Jerusalem to deliver the contribution. He then hopes to visit the Roman believers, enjoy their company, and be helped onward, asking prayer that he come in joy and find rest.

l: Phoebe, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Phoebe is a sister and servant of the assembly at Cenchreae, commended by Paul, who asks recipients to receive her worthily and assist her needs, since she has helped many, including Paul.

l: Prisca, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Prisca, a fellow worker of Paul in Christ Jesus, is greeted with Aquila; together they risked their necks for Paul's life, earning thanks from all Gentile assemblies, and host an assembly in their house.

l: Aquila, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Aquila, Paul's fellow worker in Christ Jesus, is greeted with Prisca in Chapter 16; they risked their necks for Paul's life, earned thanks from Gentile assemblies, and host an assembly in their house.

l: divisive people, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: Divisive people cause divisions and stumbling contrary to learned doctrine; recipients should watch and avoid them. Paul says they serve their own belly, not Christ, deceiving innocent hearts with smooth, flattering speech.

l: Tertius, Paul’s Letter to the Romans
s: is_a writer of the letter Tertius identifies himself as the one who writes the letter and sends his own greeting in the Lord.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: This document is Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians, in sixteen chapters, written (with Sosthenes named in the greeting) to the assembly of God at Corinth. Its central concern is a divided, puffed-up community that needs correction, and the letter moves from unity to conduct, worship, and hope. It opens with thanks for the grace given in Christ, then pleads for unity after Chloe's household reported factions claiming Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. Paul argues that the cross is God's power and wisdom, though it seems foolishness to the world, and that boasting belongs only in the Lord. Chapters 2 to 4 develop this: he came in weakness, speaking God's Spirit-revealed wisdom; the Corinthians are still fleshly babies; he and Apollos are mere servants, God gives the increase, and Christ is the foundation. Paul calls himself their father in Christ, sends Timothy, and warns he may come with a rod or in love. Chapters 5 and 6 address discipline and conduct: a man living with his father's wife must be put out, since yeast leavens the whole lump; lawsuits before unbelievers are rebuked; and the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought with a price. Chapter 7 answers their written questions on marriage, singleness, separation, and remaining in one's calling. Chapters 8 to 10 treat food sacrificed to idols: knowledge puffs up but love builds up, believers must not cause a weak brother to stumble, Paul defends his apostleship and his giving up of rights for the Good News, and Israel's wilderness failures serve as warnings against idolatry. Chapters 11 to 14 concern gatherings: head coverings, abuses at the Lord's supper with the tradition of bread and cup, and the Spirit's varied gifts given for the common good, like members of one body. Chapter 13 exalts love as greater than faith and hope. Chapter 14 prefers prophecy to uninterpreted languages and ends with order in meetings. Chapter 15 restates the Good News of Christ's death and resurrection, appearances including to Paul himself, argues against denying resurrection, and describes the imperishable body and final victory over death. Chapter 16 closes with a weekly collection for the saints in Jerusalem, Paul's travel plans via Ephesus and Macedonia, instructions about Timothy, Apollos, and Stephanas's household, final greetings, and a blessing of grace and love.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Paul is an apostle of Jesus Christ, called through the will of God, who writes to the Corinthian believers together with his companion Sosthenes, described as a brother. The records present him as a founding figure and father to the Corinthians: he planted them as a servant of God, laid a foundation as a wise master builder by the grace given him, and became their father in Christ Jesus through the Good News. He is also a fellow worker of God, a servant of Christ and steward of God's mysteries alongside Apollos, and he defends his apostleship by noting he has seen Jesus Christ as Lord and that the Corinthians are his work in the Lord. The letter opens with thanks and a plea to end divisions. Paul says Christ sent him to preach the Good News, not to baptize, so he baptized only Crispus, Gaius and the household of Stephanas. He preaches Christ crucified, not in wisdom of words. He fed the Corinthians milk rather than solid food, and says the boasting in men is wrong, though all things, including Paul, are theirs. What matters most is his conduct and self-understanding. He does not judge himself, since the Lord is his judge. He endures hunger, thirst, nakedness, beatings and homelessness, works with his own hands, and answers cursing and persecution with blessing and endurance. He has an apostolic right to financial support but does not use it, preaching without charge and under the necessity of a stewardship entrusted to him. Though free from all, he makes himself a servant to all, becoming as Jews, those under the law, those without law, and the weak, to gain them. He disciplines his body to avoid disqualification and seeks the profit of the many that they may be saved. He is unmarried and wishes others were like him, distinguishing his own judgment from the Lord's command, and thinks he has God's Spirit. He also judges a case of sexual sin within the assembly, though not outsiders. The letter moves toward plans. He sends Timothy to remind the Corinthians of his ways, which he teaches in every assembly, and says he will come shortly if the Lord is willing, asking whether they want him to come with a rod or in love and gentleness. He will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost, where a great and effective door is open despite many adversaries, then pass through Macedonia to visit them. He gives instructions on the collection, commends Timothy and the house of Stephanas, and urges Apollos to visit. He closes with a greeting written in his own hand and love for the Corinthians in Christ Jesus.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The assembly of God at Corinth is a community of believers addressed in Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians. They are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called saints, called by God into fellowship with Jesus Christ, and enriched in all speech and knowledge, lacking no gift. Most of the record concerns their problems and the correction they receive. Chloe's household reported divisions and contentions, with members claiming allegiance to Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. Paul reminds them that not many were wise, mighty, or noble by the flesh, and he rests their faith on God's power rather than human wisdom. The record unfolds as a series of rebukes and instructions. In the early chapters they are called fleshly babies in Christ, yet also God's fellow workers, God's building and temple, indwelt by the Spirit, and Christ's. Some are puffed up and boasting, and Paul, who calls them his beloved children, asks whether he should come with a rod or in gentleness. They are rebuked for arrogance over sin among them and told to purge the wicked man, and for suing one another. They are told to remain in the condition in which they were called, since they were bought with a price and should not become bondservants of men, and that the time is short, so they should live free from worldly cares. Formerly heathen led away to mute idols, they are commanded to flee idolatry and avoid fellowship with demons, and are given guidance on eating food. Their gatherings are criticized because of divisions, and many are weak, sickly, or have died. They are one body because they share one loaf, the body of Christ with members individually. They are zealous for spiritual gifts, are urged to seek the best ones, and are given instructions for orderly worship and for building up the assembly. The record ends on the Good News they received: they stand in it and are saved if they hold firmly to it. Some deny the resurrection, which would leave them in their sins if Christ had not been raised. Paul closes by calling them beloved brothers to be steadfast, immovable, and abounding in the Lord's work.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Jesus Christ, as presented across Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians, is the Son of God and Lord, the central figure of the believers' faith. The letter opens by calling him Lord and Son of God, into whose fellowship the Corinthians were called; he is the power and wisdom of God, made to believers wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Paul determines to know only him crucified, the Lord of glory whom the rulers of this world crucified in ignorance. He is the one foundation laid, the believers are his, and he belongs to God. Apostles are his servants, and Paul became the Corinthians' father in Christ Jesus. He is called our Passover, sacrificed in our place, and the one Lord through whom are all things. He died for the weak brother, so wounding believers' consciences is sinning against him. He is identified as the spiritual rock that followed the fathers in the wilderness. The Lord's table shares his blood and body, and on the night he was betrayed he gave the words of the new covenant in his blood. He is head of every man, with God as his head, and the church is his body with many members. The fullest account comes in chapter 15: he died for sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the twelve, over five hundred brothers, James, all the apostles, and last to Paul. He is the first fruits of those asleep, the second man from heaven and the last Adam, a life-giving spirit, who gives life to all in Christ. He must reign until all enemies are under his feet, then deliver the Kingdom to God the Father and himself be subjected to God. The letter closes with the prayer 'Come, Lord!', a curse on anyone who does not love him, and a wish for his grace and Paul's love in Christ Jesus to be with the Corinthians.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: God, as portrayed across Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians, is the faithful one God and Father, the source of all things, who is head of Christ and father of Christ. The records present him as the central actor behind salvation and church life. He calls believers into fellowship with his Son and in peace, and he does not allow temptation beyond their ability, providing a way of escape. His foolishness is wiser than men and his weakness stronger than men. He chooses the foolish, weak, lowly and despised to shame the wise and strong, and he made the world's wisdom foolish, so that no flesh boasts before him. The account unfolds in stages. Early chapters show him revealing his foreordained wisdom through the Holy Spirit to Paul and those with him, giving the increase to what Paul planted and Apollos watered, and regarding worldly wisdom as worthless. His believers are his fellow workers, farming, building and temple, and he will destroy anyone who destroys that temple. He will give each person praise when the Lord comes and judges those outside. Middle chapters stress that he raised Jesus and will raise believers by his power, will bring the belly and foods to nothing, and that believers were bought with a price and should glorify him. He is the one God, the Father, of whom are all things; he knows those who love him; and he was displeased with most of the Israelites overthrown in the wilderness. In the chapters on the assembly, he works all things in all, sets each member in the body as he desired, and composes the body by giving more honor to the inferior part to prevent division. He appointed apostles, prophets, teachers and others. He is not a God of confusion but of peace, and an unbeliever convicted by prophecy declares that God is among the assembly. The records close with the climax: God raised Christ, gives each seed a body as it pleased him, subjected all things to Christ except himself, and will receive the Kingdom from Christ so that God may be all in all, giving believers victory through the Lord Jesus Christ.

l: Apollos, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Apollos is a servant of God and fellow worker, called brother, through whom the Corinthians believed. Some Corinthians claimed to follow him. He watered what Paul planted, and he and Paul are the same, each rewarded for his own labor. Later, Paul urged him to visit Corinth; he declined for now but will come when able.

l: household of Stephanas, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Stephanas's household, first fruits of Achaia, devoted itself to serving the saints. Paul urges the Corinthians to submit to such people, and rejoices when Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus arrive, supplying what the Corinthians lacked and refreshing spirits.

l: divisions and contentions in Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Divisions in Corinth arose as groups claimed allegiance to Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ. In Chapter 1, Paul, informed by Chloe's household, urges unity of mind and judgment, rebuking the factions with pointed questions. In Chapter 3, he returns to the Paul-versus-Apollos factions, citing jealousy and strife as proof the believers are fleshly.

l: cross of Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The word of the cross, preached by Paul as Christ crucified, is foolishness to those dying and a stumbling block to Jews, yet God's power to those being saved; Paul avoids wisdom of words so it isn't voided.

l: wisdom of the world, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The wisdom of the world, per Paul's First Corinthians chapter 1, failed to know God through its wisdom; God will destroy it, has made it foolish, and chose foolish things to shame the wise.

l: Holy Spirit, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The Holy Spirit is presented as the Spirit from God who searches all things, including God's deep things, and uniquely knows them. In Chapter 2, he reveals God's hidden wisdom, teaches the words spoken, and is received by believers so they may know what God freely gave. In Chapter 6, he dwells in believers, whose bodies are his temple, and they were justified in him. In Chapter 12, he enables confessing Jesus as Lord, produces all varied gifts, distributes them to each as he desires, and baptizes all believers into one body.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Paul is the speaker-author of a series of letter passages addressed to the brothers, the Corinthian believers. He presents himself as an apostle, the least of them, unworthy of the name because he formerly persecuted the assembly of God, yet by God's grace, which was not futile, he worked more than all of them. The records open with his arrival among the Corinthians in weakness, fear, and trembling, proclaiming God's testimony without excellence of speech, in a demonstration of the Spirit and power. He speaks God's wisdom among the full grown, having received the Spirit from God and sharing Christ's mind. He urges the brothers to imitate him as he imitates Christ, and he delivers the traditions, including the account of the Lord's supper, which he received from the Lord. He uses himself as an example of love's necessity: without it his eloquence, knowledge, and sacrifice count for nothing. He knows in part and sees dimly now but will know fully; as a man he has put away childish things. He speaks other languages more than the Corinthians, yet prefers five words with understanding in the assembly and wants them to prophesy. He claims his writings are the Lord's commandment. Finally, he recalls preaching the Good News, says he dies daily, mentions fighting animals at Ephesus hypothetically, tells the mystery of the change at the last trumpet, and exhorts steadfastness.

l: God's wisdom, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: God's wisdom is a hidden mystery, foreordained by God before the worlds for believers' glory, unknown to this world's rulers, spoken among the full grown, revealed through the Spirit, and foolishness to the natural man.

l: human wisdom, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: is_not_basis_of faith [Paul's preaching aimed that faith not stand in it] Human wisdom is contrasted with God's wisdom: the speaker did not use persuasive words of it, so that faith would not rest on the wisdom of men. It is described as the wisdom of this world and its rulers, who are coming to nothing. The words the speaker uses are not taught by it but by the Holy Spirit.

l: foundation (laid by Paul, Jesus Christ), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Paul, as a wise master builder, laid the foundation by the grace of God, and it is Jesus Christ. No one can lay any other foundation, though others build on it and must be careful how they do so.

l: each man's work (building on the foundation), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Each man's work, built on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or straw, will be revealed by the Day and tested by fire. If it remains, the builder receives a reward. If it is burned, he suffers loss but is himself saved, as through fire.

l: worldly wisdom, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: is foolishness with God The wisdom of this world is declared foolishness with God, and anyone who thinks himself wise in it must become a fool in order to become wise. Scripture is cited that God takes the wise in their craftiness and knows their reasoning is worthless.

l: Timothy, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Timothy is Paul's beloved, faithful child who does the Lord's work as Paul does. Paul asks the Corinthians to receive him without fear, let no one despise him, and send him onward in peace, since Paul expects him with the brothers.

l: Lord, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The Lord is presented as an authority figure. In Chapter 4 he judges Paul and will come to reveal hidden things and hearts' counsels, and Paul's visit depends on his willingness. In Chapter 7 he commands spouses not to separate, the unmarried seek to please him, and a called bondservant is his free man.

l: the apostles, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The apostles are stewards required to be faithful, yet displayed last of all like men sentenced to death and made a spectacle to world, angels and men. They are fools for Christ, weak, dishonored, deprived and beaten, yet bless those who curse them.

l: God’s Kingdom, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: God's Kingdom is said not to be inherited by the unrighteous, a point stated twice and illustrated by a list including the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, drunkards, slanderers and extortionists.

l: Good News, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The Good News is the message Paul preaches, which the Lord ordained should support those who proclaim it. In Chapter 9, Paul preaches under necessity, declines support, offers it free, and acts for its sake to share in it. In Chapter 15, it is what the brothers received and are saved by if they hold firm. Its core is that Christ died for sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, confirmed by many appearances.

l: judgment, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: timing reserved until the Lord comes [people should judge nothing before then] Paul says human judgment of him is a very small thing and that he does not even judge himself, because the Lord is his judge. The Corinthians are told to judge nothing before the Lord comes, who will expose hidden things and the counsels of hearts, after which each will receive praise from God.

l: pride and boasting, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: is_unwarranted_because everything is received Paul says the Corinthians are puffed up against one another and asks what they have that they did not receive, questioning why they boast. He says some are puffed up as though he would not come, and that he will test not their words but their power.

l: assembly of God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The assembly of God is the Corinthian gathering, which belongs to God. In Chapter 11 it is marked by divisions and factions, and Paul faults the members for despising it, shaming the poor, and failing to wait for one another. In Chapter 14 it is the place where gifts build up the body: orderly prophecy convicts visitors, who then worship God.

l: man who has his father's wife, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: has father's wife [sexual relationship] This man is reported to have his father's wife, and Paul has already judged him. The believers are instructed to deliver him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus, and to put him away from among them.

l: sexual immorality, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Sexual immorality is a sin reported among Corinthian believers, of a kind not even named among the Gentiles: a man having his father's wife. Paul clarifies that his earlier warning to avoid sexual sinners meant professing brothers, not the world's. It is later listed among behaviors excluding people from God's Kingdom; readers must flee it, since the body is for the Lord and the immoral person sins against his own body.

l: yeast, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: effect leavens the whole lump [even a little] Yeast serves as a metaphor: a little yeast leavens the whole lump, illustrating how one sinner's influence affects the community. Believers are told to purge out the old yeast and to keep the feast not with the yeast of malice and wickedness but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

l: erring brothers (immoral believers), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Anyone called a brother who is a sexual sinner, covetous, an idolater, a slanderer, a drunkard, or an extortionist is not to be associated with, and the believers are not even to eat with such a person. Unlike outsiders, whom God judges, these within the community are to be judged by the believers.

l: saints, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The saints are destined to judge the world and even angels; the writer argues this future role makes them fit to settle minor everyday disputes themselves rather than before the unrighteous.

l: the unrighteous, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: will_not_inherit God's Kingdom The unrighteous are those before whom believers wrongly take their lawsuits, and the writer describes them as of no account in the assembly. They will not inherit God's Kingdom, and a list of sins, including sexual immorality, idolatry, theft, drunkenness and extortion, characterizes them.

l: lawsuits among believers, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: A rebuke of believers who sue one another before unbelievers: the writer shames readers for lacking a wise arbiter, calls such lawsuits already a defect, and says being wronged or defrauded is better.

l: Corinthian believers (the readers), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The Corinthian believers are the recipients of Paul's letter, a community addressed with rebuke, reminder, and instruction. Early on they are shamed for lawsuits before unbelievers and for wronging and defrauding brothers, yet reminded they were washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, are members of Christ, and were bought with a price, so they should flee sexual immorality and glorify God in their bodies. Next they are called the seal of Paul's apostleship, with an argument about material support and an exhortation to run the race to win. Finally they receive practical directions: weekly saving for the collection, receiving Timothy, honoring laborers like the house of Stephanas, standing firm in love, and exchanging greetings.

l: Jesus, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Jesus is called the Lord, in whose name the readers were justified. God raised him up, believers' bodies are members of Christ, and the one joined to the Lord is one spirit with him. Jesus is named in the test of speaking by God's Spirit: no one speaking by the Spirit says "Jesus is accursed." Saying "Jesus is Lord" is possible only by the Holy Spirit.

l: body, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The believer's body is for the Lord, not sexual immorality; God will raise it. As a member of Christ and temple of the Holy Spirit, bought with a price, it should glorify God.

l: marriage, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Marriage, in Chapter 7, is a remedy for sexual immorality and lack of self-control, better than burning with passion. It is not sin, though Paul says it brings fleshly oppression and divided concern, so he prefers staying unmarried. A wife is bound while her husband lives.

l: husbands, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Husbands, as described in Chapter 7, owe their wives affection and lack authority over their own bodies, which belong to the wife. They are commanded by the Lord not to leave their wives, even unbelieving ones content to stay, and married men worry about pleasing their wives.

l: wives, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Wives are addressed in Chapter 7 as a group bound to their husbands: they must give affection, not leave them, and lack authority over their own bodies. If separated, they stay unmarried or reconcile. Married wives concern themselves with pleasing husbands; widows may remarry in the Lord, though Paul thinks staying single is happier.

l: unmarried and widows, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: In Chapter 7, Paul advises the unmarried and widows to remain unmarried as he is, concerned with pleasing the Lord and spared marriage's troubles, but free to marry if they lack self-control.

l: celibacy and self-control, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Celibacy is a gift from God that Paul, in Chapter 7, considers good and better than marriage. Those lacking self-control should marry; couples may briefly abstain by consent for prayer, avoiding Satan's temptation. Paul offers this as concession and judgment, not commandment.

l: calling, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The calling is a teaching that each person should remain in the condition in which God called them, whether circumcised or not, bondservant or free. Keeping God's commandments matters most; a bondservant may take an opportunity for freedom. Paul says this rule applies in all assemblies.

l: things sacrificed to idols, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: effect_on_conscience_of_the_weak defiles [when eaten by the weak with consciousness of an idol] Eating things sacrificed to idols is the topic of the chapter. Food in itself does not commend anyone to God, since not eating makes one no worse and eating makes one no better, yet some eat it as a thing sacrificed to an idol and are defiled in conscience, and others may be emboldened to eat it.

l: idols, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: is_a nothing in the world Idols are said to be nothing in the world. Although many so-called gods and lords exist in heaven and on earth, believers have only one God and one Lord. Some people, with consciousness of an idol until now, still treat the food as belonging to an idol, and an idol's temple is the place where a person with knowledge might be seen sitting.

l: knowledge, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Knowledge is contrasted with love: it puffs up while love builds up, is not present in all men, and one person's knowledge can cause a weak brother to perish.

l: love, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Love is presented as the quality that gives value to every gift and sacrifice; without it the speaker is nothing. It is patient, kind, not envious, boastful, proud, self-seeking or easily provoked, keeps no account of evil, rejoices with truth, and bears, believes, hopes and endures all things. It never fails, remains after prophecy, languages and knowledge pass away, and is greatest of faith, hope and love.

l: the weak (weak believers), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Weak believers are brothers for whom Christ died, lacking knowledge about idols and holding a conscience tied to them. Seeing the knowledgeable eat in an idol's temple emboldens them to eat, defiling their conscience and risking their perishing.

l: those with knowledge (the strong), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The strong, those with knowledge, know no idol is anything and that there is one God. They are warned their liberty must not stumble the weak, since wounding conscience sins against Christ; the writer models this by vowing to eat no meat.

l: conscience, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: determines abstaining from food declared offered to idols [the other person's conscience] Conscience is the basis for eating without questions what is sold in the butcher shop or set before one at an unbeliever's meal. If someone says the food was offered to idols, one should not eat it for the sake of that person's conscience, not one's own. The speaker asks why his liberty should be judged by another's conscience.

l: apostolic right to financial support, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Apostolic right to financial support is held by Barnabas, Paul, and Cephas, and exercised over the Corinthians by others, though Paul has it more. Paul defends it with examples of soldiers, planters, shepherds, the ox in Moses' law, and temple servants, and the Lord's ordinance, yet he and Barnabas did not use it.

l: race and athletic games, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Paul uses the race as a metaphor: all run but only one wins the prize. Athletes discipline themselves for a corruptible crown, believers for an incorruptible one. He urges running to win, and disciplines his own body to avoid disqualification.

l: Paul's preaching without charge, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: is_reward_of Paul [his reward] Paul says his reward is presenting the Good News of Christ without charge, so as not to abuse his authority in it. He would rather die than have anyone make his boasting void, and he says he has used none of his rights. He bears all things so as to cause no hindrance to the Good News.

l: our fathers (Israelites in the wilderness), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: The fathers, Israelites in the wilderness, all shared the cloud, sea crossing, baptism into Moses, and spiritual food and drink. Yet most displeased God and fell through lust, idolatry, immorality, testing Christ, and grumbling, so their experiences serve as examples and warnings for believers.

l: idolatry, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: Idolatry is cited as a sin of some of the fathers, who sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play. The brothers are told to flee from it. The speaker says an idol or a thing sacrificed to idols is nothing in itself, yet the sacrifices are made to demons.

l: demons, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
s: receive Gentile sacrifices [not God] The Gentiles' sacrifices are said to be offered to demons and not to God. The speaker does not want the brothers to have fellowship with demons and says they cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons, or partake of both tables.
